Review Time!
I do recommend this game.  I love old Final Fantasy inspired games.  And I like how the classes are clearly defined and color coded so you know exactly what is for each class.
Now just because I have certain troubles with a game, I not one to give a bad review.
With that being said I hate using a controller for this game, half of my controller just didn't work. And for this style game I need to use the D-pad but I was forced to use the analogue stick.  So I just had to use the keyboard for this game. =(
But other than that I'm loving this game.  And I quite enjoy the music.  Oh yeah I love the fact that it doesn't ask me if I want to save over my old game every time I want to save!  And the humor at least for me has me laughing out loud.

One of the best RPG Maker titles out there. It has a unique story with well-written characters that you actually care about. Don't let the simple graphics fool you - there's real heart and craft here. A must-play for JRPG fans who appreciate a good story.

This was such a charming throwback to JRPGs from the NES and even the SNES era.  

It had surprising depth and it managed to capture some of the "simplicity" of the games from those eras, while reducing or eliminating a lot of the grind or tedium that those games had (ex: think Final Fantasy 1: endless walking, fights that drag on forever, hitting empty spaces after monsters are killed in combat, or dying in combat and having to *redo  30+ minutes of gameplay to get back to where you were before).

You can tell the game was made with a lot of care and love, and while not perfect, highly recommended for fans of old-school JRPGs or gamers that grew up in the 80s or 90s!

Minor gripes:
1) I grew to really appreciate the art style, but at the beginning I felt like some assets looked more like console "blocky" 8-bit, while others looked like assets made in MS Paint with higher detail; not bad by any means, but visually it felt like conflicting styles.
2) While they did do a really good job at reducing tedium, you should still expect to spend a lot of time walking, dealing with many random encounters and lots of fights that you can't just "fast-foward" through as if you were using an emulator.  I think it's hard to avoid this when you are creating a game in reverence to these types of old JRPGs, but you may start to feel this before the end of the game, especially if you "binge" the game over a few of days.
3) I encountered a few bugs, all of them minor but I still noticed.  Later in the game there many walls you could walk through that should have been solid imo, as they did not lead to any secrets.  And one time when exiting a dungeon, something weird happened with the tiles I could move my character to, but after entering/exiting the dungeon again, everything worked well.

Overall though, I love this game, and it really suprised me at times with its creativity, and yet also its faithfulness and references to the games of the past.

Final rating: 85/100

I highly recommend and will be getting the sequel soon.

I really enjoyed my time with this game. (my hours are from three separate starts/restarts over a few years). You did a lot with very little and some very amazing PoV sorcery on some scenes and areas. Great use of parallax and music. The combat, though a bit repetitive, was well balanced (until the very end but that's to be expected in a jrpg style game). I thought bosses were reasonably difficult, I even died a few times. The only character I struggled to find use until late game was the Thief, outside of her poison and smoke bomb abilities. I felt that the element system, built into the very world & individuals within it, was a unique take and I loved the concept of the BBEG. It was a very interesting story that I enjoyed a lot with a lot of side quests. I loved that each piece of ultimate gear was locked behind some sort of legend or side quest that you could ignore if you wanted but I really wanted to seek out. (except for the last three pieces of course). I felt that your dungeon design was very well done with an appropriate amount of encounters & twists/turns with treasures. I feel like most items mattered and I was mostly almost broke until the very end of the game (which is good from a balancing place imo). I thoroughly enjoyed the dev room trivia section as a hobbyist game maker myself. It is fun to peer behind the veil of what other people's development process is like. I'm going to be vague about the ending but basically my main criticism is having to use an item several times & then not really feeling like the cool abilities I unlocked at level 20 were really that effective on the last boss. I think you were going for a "this boss should feel unbeatable and what these characters should feel is dread that their strongest abilities are doing very low damage to it... can we win this?" and then the umm *vague on purpose* where you aren't really able to fight anymore but just heal was a bold choice. If the feeling you were going for was to make the player feel like this is a lost cause then it worked but idk, I think you might have sacrificed their heroic persona for the big reveal at the end. It was cool, don't get me wrong, just not sure how I feel about it. I really enjoyed my time in this world and am looking forward to playing through the sequel next!

Decent intro to the excellent 8-Bit Adventures 2.  This one's simpler, rather short (9 hours or so for 100%), and far less polished, but still a decent game if you want a short RPG.

The graphics here are definitely NES style, with similar color limits.  Battle sprites are VERY pixelated, which actually matters (and helps) due to the color system.  Sound design is fine, and music's solid.  If you played the sequel you'd recognize some of the tracks or some of what became songs in the second game.

The battle system is simple turn based affair, similar to Dragon Quest, but with a twist that most enemies and all the player characters have a color associated with them.  Red beats Green, Green beats Blue, and Blue beats Red.  Each character's normal attack is associated with their color, each skill has a color tag assoicated with it, and these colors drastically affect how much damage you can do and how much enemies do to you.  Buffs and debuffs are powerful, as in the sequel, but it's rather difficult to land some debuffs on late game foes and bosses.  Debuffs used by foes can be extremely dangerous, blind especially is very punishing.

The story is fine, with a few interesting twists.  Since I played the sequel first (as it was a gift), most of the events of this title were spoiled.  It was still interesting to see some of the threads that would be closed up in the sequel get started; and it was neat seeing young Charlie before he started his adventure in the sequel.

Techwise it's probably fine if you're on Windows, but there are a few issues on Linux.  It uses MS Core fonts, which cannot be distributed by Valve so by default you won't get damage numbers.  This can be fixed with Protontricks, for Deck users and those uncomfortable with the command line there's a guide that walks through the process of installing them.  For those comfortable with the command line use:
[code]protontricks 370300 corefonts[/code]
to install the set of MS core fonts.  Make sure to run the game once to set up the proton prefix.  The sequel does not have this issue.

Controller was a little weird, I had to remap things with SteamInput (you can try the F1 menu as well), and it wouldn't always stay full screen, but that's fixed with a simple alt-tab.  Finally there were a few map related glitches, mostly around the Dwarven cave.

Still worth a play if you have any interest in, or played the sequel.  Definitely play the sequel, it improves on the mechanics, visuals, and storytelling in so many ways.

Like the title implies, 8-bit adventures encompasses the classic rpg games from the late 80's to early 90's through it's art style and feel. Unlike other game of that era it dumbs down the complexity a bit by having a cap on the amount of abilities you can learn for each character and boiling down the elemental traits to a rock-paper-scissors like system. This is by NO means a bad thing, if anything it makes combat more approachable and so you don't have to guess or memorize the weakness of each enemy. It also devoids the feeling that you need to constantly grind for levels; you could do the minimal amount of combat and not be overwhelmed. The story itself is simple, fun and somewhat serious.

Even though it only took me 12 hour to 100% it, I still felt satisfied with it. It just shows that not all jrpgs need be lengthy and grindy to enjoy them.

That being said, having played both this and 8-bit Adventures 2 (which is a direct sequel to this game), while #1 is good, #2 a wonderful game, and is superior to #1 in every imaginable way. You don't need to have played #1 to get or enjoy #2; but if you're like me and played #2 and were then curious about #1, you'll find that the story, characters, and mechanics of #2 are thoroughly enriched by experiencing #1.

8-bit Adventures: The Forgotten Journey is a game that should always be remembered. As a faithful, fun, and just as engaging JRPG as the ones it takes homage from (like Final Fantasy). It's in the name, after all, with all the graphics being 8-bit.

You play as a Warrior, Thief, and Mage team (names you can decide for yourself) as they are brought together by an omnipotent force to save the world. Seems basic stuff, but the characters have nice banter and chemistry that makes it more endearing. The Warrior is a knight captain who is very trusting and a bit silly in how he wants to ride an airship. The Thief is a snarky girl with her heart closed up and takes the longest to warm up. The Mage is at least two centuries old, is wise about the world, and even has his own struggles he tries to bury in the past. And when you get your three colored orbs that represent the world, you are tasked to find a weapon that can stop the foreign enemy known as Dust.

And might I say, it's very clever that the omnipotent god, the Computer, has the most dangerous enemy being Dust. Writing like this is very clever. As well as showing how grim and damaging the dust is by corrupting the world, especially in the Game Kid world.

I adore this game, having played it twice over. The first time was on Steam Deck with some limitations of no achievements unlocked, and somehow beat it without any indicator of numbers when I dealt damage. The second time was easier reading the damage numbers work as intended, but the game is still greatly put together.

Fortunately the game is simple to learn and master. Each character has their own skills geared to a preference, as well as their color element in a rock paper scissors format. Blue, to Red, to Green, to Blue again. The Warrior has damaging moves plus an attack buff and all healing spells, the Thief has subversive attacks like poison, stun and steal (which you can use to get extra potions for HP and MP), and the Mage has spells of the three elements that go up in tiers. And despite being color coded, they have skills in other colors. The Mage is most obvious using Fire, Water and Wind, but the Warrior and Thief also get a small section of damaging moves outside their usual element.

8-Bit Adventure is kind of on the short side, but it flows well from point to point. You get an airship pretty quickly, but you won't be able to have it land on any point of the world yet. And when you get close to fighting the Dust at the end, the world REALLY opens up with a whole slew of side quests to get the ultimate equipment and a bit more lore of the character's backstories. 

I can't recommend this enough, as it feels like a true love letter to the classics and still telling a story that is both something old and something new. Helps that it's on the cheaper side of the price point, and even has a sequel!

Остановился на 8-Bit Adventures 1 по причине того, что события в ней сорвались с места в карьер и быстро увлекли меня простотой процесса. "8-Bit Adventures: The Forgotten Journey" is a single dev JRPG made in RPG-Maker and an earnest bow to the classics, while inheriting a "meta"-narrative that is worth the journey.

On the surface you have your standard fantasy tropes with the typical main protagonists bound to save the world - pretty standard stuff, but they are quite likeable. 

Presentationwise it is a really "blocky" experience. The pixelated surroundings are really simple, their scaling sometimes feels off and they got some asset-characteristics. Spritework is also very basic and the enemy design is so awkwardly plain, that it nearly inherits a style of its own (last boss looks cool, though). The writing is quite decent; I found minor typos, but nothing severe. Music is also nice, simple and retro.

Gameplaywise you get your standard-combat mechanics with elemental weaknesses, it gets the job done (the "SmokeScreen"-Ability feels really strong for normal mobs and you got this from the start). Luckily it is not very grindy and has almost no backtracking. Escaping battles has a good window of success.

The overarching narrative and the symbolism of it [spoiler] the inevitability of the old to catch dust and your ability to prevent this [/spoiler] got me through the whole ordeal which can be casually 100% in less than 10 hours.

Overall a nice and heartfelt little game that can be offputting for some, but nevertheless gets the oldschool-charm right.

Cool little homage to old school NES rpg's with some QOL features added in, such as being able to save anywhere at any point, to offset the fact that for some reason when you level up your HP and MP aren't automatically restored like in most games of this sort. 

The story starts out pretty basic, but then does a few interesting things you might not expect, though I have to say that one of the twists didn't have the impact it would've had on me if I handn't randomly played the Evoland duology very recently and seen something similar.

IMO, it's a bit too simplistic in its visual style, going for a very early NES graphics style instead of something a bit more sophisticated reminiscent of later NES games, such as what you see in other 8-bit retro games like Breath of Death VII and the 8-bit portions of Evoland 2, which look significantly better, along with stuff like Dragon Quest V on my cellphone. 

Anyway, barring those minor gripes, it's a solid game of this style, with a lot of heart and some room for improvement as far as game mechanics are concerned. I hear the sequel is much better, so I'll be sure to give it a try.

Edit: Now that I've finished it, I have to say that it was better than I originally gave it credit for. The final boss was handled in a very unusual and interesting way. It was really tough, especially because it has a couple of gimmicks you probably won't figure out at first, and after you finally beat it after a bunch of transformations it comes back yet again for another fight that has a few surprises thrown in. Very well done.

An absolute master class in indie / old school game design.
I can't say enough good things about this game and it's sequel. From music, to pacing, to writing, and tor story telling. This is a remarkable evolution of the old school rpg genre. I did not expect to find such depth in such a simple looking package. If you grew up in the era of FF1, Dragon Quest and Lufia, then this will warm all the right Nostalgia buttons while bringing a fresh sense of humor and fun to the genre. 
If this is your first time, experimenting with this type of game, then you will get to see the best of old school gaming techniques where clever writing and music are used to stir your imagination to fill the graphical gaps, and bring you along, literally on an unforgettable adventure. Give this a go and I am sure, you will want to dive right into the sequel. And if you are coming to this from the sequel then you are going to love seeing where it all began.
The only flaw I see in this game is that it had the misfortune of coming out in the same year as so many other amazing games.

While the game is a bit jank and falls to some of the indie RPG trappings like the references kind of sapping the game's own identity, I really ended up liking it, especially towards the end. It's a very simple JRPG, the writing is generally well though out and easily understandable and there were even a few turns that I wasn't expecting. The world and dialogue has lot of charm and personality and the little world in it is varied and quite fun to explore even if there really isn't all that much depth persay. You've got a party of three with no customization beyond just upgrading equipment and the combat is about as basic as it gets but I think it gets the job done for its ~10 hour run time. For the visuals I find the enemy designs to be a bit too amateurish for my liking, but the overworld and 8-bit style character graphics I find to be quite nice and there's tons of little details here and there, and the music was also pretty good, the mage tower theme in particular stood out for me.

I do also have to mention that using a controller on this game is a major pain thanks to its RPG Maker roots, after fiddling around I managed to get the controller working but I could not change the configurations no matter how hard I tried, so I had to play the game with the cancel/menu button being tied to start, annoying for sure, but I learned to deal with it.

It's hardly perfect, but if you are in the lookout for a short charming old school JRPG you could do a whole lot worse than playing this. The sequel is also definitely on my radar now after playing this.

8-Bit Adventures 1: The Forgotten Journey is an excellent homage to classic JRPGS.

First, it's important that I mention all of my hours were played on Steam Deck, which works, but requires some setup. Be advised... there is a glitch when playing this game on Steam Deck that prevents any damage numbers from appearing in battles. This may be a deal breaker for some, however, I did not find this to be game breaking in any way as the combat is intuitive enough that anyone with previous JRPG experience can estimate how much damage attacks are doing with some accuracy. I played through the entire game working around this glitch, and while some battles probably took longer than if I could see the actual numbers, it was still an enjoyable experience.

To enjoy this game on the deck, first you'll have to configure one of your keys as F1 on the keyboard, which allows you to access the controller setup. Follow the community guide to set up the controller to behave as expected. Once that's done, go back into the Steam Deck controller settings for the game and change the default behavior of the D-Pad to mimic the Left Stick. Then you'll be able to use the D-Pad for character movement. Upon loading the game each time, you'll need to move the mouse cursor out of the way. This isn't as annoying as it seems, and aside from moving the mouse cursor, you only need to set this up one time. Trust me, this game is worth it.

As a retro homage, this game does a fantastic job with it's graphics, sound, and gameplay.

Now, the story... I can't say much without spoiling anything, but it vastly exceeded my expectations. To be honest, I wasn't expecting much in the way of story, I was expecting it to be a bit gimmicky. However, what I experienced was a story that actually had me coming back excited to find out what was going to happen next. Dare I say, the story was far more interesting than most of the 8-bit classics that it drew inspiration from. I've done a fair bit of game hopping lately, losing interest in titles before I'm able to complete them, but 8-Bit Adventures had me interested and entertained until the very end. I will be purchasing the sequel based on the strength of this title alone.

The only con for me... The enemy designs were overly simplistic at times. But this was also part of the charm in a way.

Even with the extra effort required to make it work on Steam Deck, and not being able to see the damage numbers, this game is a strong recommend from me. Definitely pick it up on sale, but worth it even at full price if you love classic JRPGS like Final Dragon and Fantasy Warrior Quest. Don't let a small thing like Steam Deck certification keep you from enjoying this game. Go for it!

A few tips that might also be a clue as to whether or not this is a good game for you:
-There are no skills/spells that heal status conditions so it would be wise to stock up on items that can.
-There are no skills/spells which provide protection against enemy magic however there are skills which can prevent the enemy from successfully attacking and they often even work on bosses.
-Curing HP is cheap and getting enough damage is important making it better for the fighter and thief to default to the weapon with the highest damage over options that boost defense or stats (the mage just wants INT - shocking, I know)
-12.8 hours was enough time to 100% the game achievements even playing at a relatively leisurely pace. Doing all the side quests will provide better equipment and more experience without wasting time.

8-Bit Adventures is a game that I honestly cannot recommend.  It can be really enjoyable in some spots.  It has a basic story, which is one of it's strengths, and the presentation is pretty good.  It's trying to pull off an 8-bit aesthetic and simplicity, reminding me of RPGs from the NES days.  However, where this game falls really flat is the combat.  I don't know how the developer did it, but I feel extremely weak all the time.  Every battle is a slog, even utilizing the basic weakness system, nearly every battle requires you to spam spells to get anywhere without taking ludicrous amounts of damage, and some bosses are just plain cheap.  The Blue Mage Tower boss comes quickly to mind with it's spell spam.  Since classic save points are around, this game would have benefited so much just from having tents; allowing the player to fully heal before boss fights, but we don't get that luxury.  Healing is few and far between and equipment upgrades are likewise extremely hard to find and get, typically only giving you a minor upgrade long after you needed it.  It also feels like your stats really don't matter other than HP and MP; having high stats seems to have minimal effect; to the point where I'm dealing only around 15-20 damage per swing with a character with over 60 Strength.  Even with the best weapons I can find, I feel extremely weak and struggle to keep up with basic enemies.  I'm still open to the sequel being better, but this entry is the biggest RPG slog I think I've ever played.

I"m just about at the end of this game, but I wanted to take some time to write out a review. Firstly, if you're one of those people who hate all RPGMaker games no matter what, or if you're one of those clowns who hate anything with a retro aesthetic, move along because this isn't for you. For the rest? Let's keep going.

Now you'd think taking RPGMaker, known mainly for games in at least a 16 bit art style, and making an 8-Bit game wouldn't work. But this game succeeds despite that. The 8-bit graphics are top notch, about as good as anything you would get back on the NES. Meanwhile, the music is OUTSTANDING. It's an absolutely exceptional soundtrack and adds to the game in every way. 

But of course a game can look and sound good, but how does it play? And more importantly, what's the story like since this is after all, an RPG?

The gameplay is fairly standard. You wander villages and dungeons, gather items, fight random encounters, and level up. You only ever have 3 party members, but they each get a variety of skills. Everyone can heal a bit, everyone can eventually learn various buffs and debuffs, and single hit and multi hit attacks. Where the trick comes in, is with the games element system. There are three colors; Red, Blue, and Green. 

Essentially, green defeats blue, blue defeats red, and red defeats green. Your characters have a normal attack for their corresponding element and special moves corresponding to the three. Examples being the Warrior (Blue) getting green and red attacks, and the Thief (green) getting blue and red attacks. The third charaters is a Mage (red) and can hit all of them in some way or another.

The trick in battle, at least early on, comes from using these skills properly along with buffs and debuffs to succeed. I say "early on" as a lead in to one of the games faults. As you level up and learn the more powerful skills, strategy doesn't become a factor as much. Late game all I needed was the warriors hit-all red/green attacks, the thiefs hit all blue/red attacks, and the mage covering the last element and the battle was on. Especially very late game where it seems some enemies don't even have elements. It's a minor point, but I wish the difficulty had been a little more consistent.

That leads to the story and the writing. It starts out super basic; three heroes, three magic orbs, save the world. If you only played the first couple of hours, then you'd think that's all your getting. However get a couple of hours in, once you have all the orbs, and the game starts going in a unique direction. I had to stop and think to myself, "did he really do that?" It's then fairly regular again until you get close to the end, where there's major character developments for everyone. And it's not just random crap like you see in some games. Nah these twists and developments are earned. After that you get to the end-game, where the writing really messes with your expectations about the villain and even some events dating back to the start of the game. 

On top of this is the whole idea that the game seems to have a "Meta" type of setting (Not Facebook, Ha). Going any further would spoil it, but if you play it you'll figure out what I mean.

All in all, this is one of the best RPGMaker titles I've had the pleasure to play. And it's inexpensive. I highly recommend that you give this one your time and enjoy it as much as I did.
